title: Which divisor estimates spread?
hook: Enumerate four tiny samples and compare two ways to estimate variance.

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: simulate small samples; dividing by n underestimates the spread.

misconception: Treating why n − 1? as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: simulate small samples; dividing by n underestimates the spread.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: A population contains 0 and 2 with equal probability. Across all size-2 samples, what is the average variance estimate using divisor n−1?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-why-n-1/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Population [0,2] equally likely; enumerate size-2 samples [0,0],[0,2],[2,0],[2,2]. Mean squared deviation with divisor n averages .5; with n-1 averages 1, equal to population variance 1.

claims.text: Dividing by n−1 retains average variance 1; dividing by n retains 0.5. The four bars enumerate all equally likely size-two samples.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-why-n-1/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Population [0,2] equally likely; enumerate size-2 samples [0,0],[0,2],[2,0],[2,2]. Mean squared deviation with divisor n averages .5; with n-1 averages 1, equal to population variance 1.

claims.text: Estimating the center from the same sample makes squared deviations too small on average. The n−1 divisor corrects that expectation under independent sampling; it does not make each individual sample variance equal the population variance.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-why-n-1/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Population [0,2] equally likely; enumerate size-2 samples [0,0],[0,2],[2,0],[2,2]. Mean squared deviation with divisor n averages .5; with n-1 averages 1, equal to population variance 1.

claims.text: A sample has squared deviations summing to 12 and n=4. What is its n−1 variance estimate? Divide 12 by 4−1=3, giving 4.
